name: Malay, 'het Djohorsch of Riouwsch' = Johor-Riau Malay
confidence_why: Every grammar from Marsden 1812 through Crawfurd 1852, Favre 1876, van Wijk 1890 and Winstedt 1945 puts the admittedly weak stress on the penult, shifting to the final syllable when the penult is an open schwa, but instrumental studies of Malaysian Malay by Zuraidah, Knowles and Yong 2008 and Wan Aslynn 2012, and the survey by Kaufman and Himmelmann, argue that this prominence is phrasal intonation and that Malay has no word stress at all, so the type of system is under active debate.
catalog_citation: van Wijk, D. Gerth. 1890. Spraakleer der Maleische taal. Batavia: G. Kolff & Co. Sec. 95-96 'Klemtoon', pp. 46-48. (Glottolog's long grammar for mala1479; Inleiding sec. 1 p. III: treats only 'het Djohorsch of Riouwsch' Malay.)
catalog_locator: Sec. 95 'Klemtoon', p. 46 of archive.org item spraakleer-der-maleische-taal; continuation sec. 96 pp. 46-48. rendered and read (p.70) checked against it.
catalog_quote: § 95. De klemtoon is in het Maleisch in het algemeen zeer zwak; alle lettergrepen, die niet geheel toonloos zijn, worden met nagenoeg denzelfden nadruk uitgesproken ... alleen op de voorlaatste of de laatste wordt wat meer klemtoon gelegd, niet zoozeer door er sterker op te drukken of de stem te verheffen, maar alleen door ze wat gerekter en langzamer uit te spreken. In het algemeen valt de klemtoon op de voorlaatste lettergreep van het stamwoord (1); alleen wanneer deze open is en een pĕpĕt heeft, komt het accent op de laatste lettergreep; dus b. v. kàta, boèroeng, tèmpat, dèndam, binàsa, bĕlàlai (2); daarentegen bĕlòm, tjĕrài, bĕnàr, pĕtjàh, djĕdjàk, bĕsàr, kĕnà, kĕnàl. Wordt echter die open toonlooze lettergreep gevolgd door ng, dan valt het accent toch meer op de penultima dan op de ultima; b. v. tèngah, dèngar; dikwijls is het bij de kleurloosheid der uitspraak moeielijk te beslissen, welke lettergreep in dit geval den klemtoon heeft, daar beide nagenoeg even lang gerekt worden; b. v. bĕngis, dĕngoeng, en de uitspraak vaak afhangt van de gemoedsstemming, waarin de spreker verkeert; zoo zal men wel gewoonlijk hooren pĕtjàh; maar wanneer met een zekere emphase gesproken wordt, hoort men juist de lettergreep pĕ wel rekken, soedah pĕtjah, al gebroken. § 96. De oorspronkelijke, natuurlijke klemtoon blijft in den regel behouden, wanneer het woord suffixen aanneemt; b. v. bànding, bàndingan; koèmpoel, koèmpoelan, dàpat, mendàpati

new_statements.quote: § 95. De klemtoon is in het Maleisch in het algemeen zeer zwak; alle lettergrepen, die niet geheel toonloos zijn, worden met nagenoeg denzelfden nadruk uitgesproken ... alleen op de voorlaatste of de laatste wordt wat meer klemtoon gelegd, niet zoozeer door er sterker op te drukken of de stem te verheffen, maar alleen door ze wat gerekter en langzamer uit te spreken. new_statements.translation: Sec. 95. Stress in Malay is in general very weak; all syllables that are not wholly toneless [schwa-syllables] are pronounced with almost the same emphasis ... only the penultimate or the last receives somewhat more stress, not so much by pressing harder on it or raising the voice, but only by pronouncing it somewhat more drawn-out and slowly. In general the stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the root word; only when this syllable is open and has a pepet [schwa] does the accent come on the last syllable; thus e.g. kàta, boèroeng, tèmpat, dèndam, binàsa, bĕlàlai; on the other hand bĕlòm, tjĕrài, bĕnàr, pĕtjàh, djĕdjàk, bĕsàr, kĕnà, kĕnàl.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Weak durational prominence on the penultimate syllable of the root; if the penult is an open syllable whose vowel is schwa (pepet), prominence falls on the final syllable instead (schwa-light penult -> final). If the open schwa penult is followed by ng (tengah, dengar) the accent stays rather on the penult, though often hard to decide. Under suffixation the root normally keeps its stress (bànding > bàndingan, koèmpoel > koèmpoelan), i.e. the domain is the root, not the suffixed word.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Sec.96 (p.47, quoting von de Wall): in educated/spelling-influenced speech a weak second 'grammatical' stress may appear on the new penult (long vowel) of suffixed forms beside the strong natural root stress (bàntoe, bàntoei, pĕrbàntoean); rarely the root stress is lost entirely (katànja < kàta, tambàngan ~ tàmbangan). Crawfurd 1852:cix adds that polysyllables have two accents, on the first and on the penultimate syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: European loans with original final accent keep it (majoòr, tamboèr); apparent antepenultimate cases manoèsia, moèlia, karoènia are really penultimate (karoènja, moèlja, manoèsja); emphasis can lengthen a schwa penult (soedah pĕtjah); shifting stress fully onto the suffix-created penult (koedànja, padànja) is called a European-Javanese habit 'never heard from the Malay'. Winstedt [1945]:4 gives the same rule for colloquial peninsular Malay ('no strong accent on any syllable'; penult, but final when penult is schwa in an open and rarely a closed syllable: sĕrì, ĕnàm, ĕntàh, ĕmpàt; root keeps its stress under suffixation). Modern instrumental work on Malaysian Malay (Zuraidah, Knowles & Yong 2008; Wan 2012) argues the apparent penult prominence is a phrase-final pitch peak plus final lengthening and that Malay has no word stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Author's domain is the root word ('stamwoord') in citation; he stresses that prominence is durational and very weak. The rule is the classic schwa-conditioned penult/final pattern (StressTyp2/Hayes treat open schwa penults as light), hence 'weight-sensitive' rather than plain fixed: penultimate syllable; a no-word-stress reading is defended by modern phoneticians for present-day Malaysian Malay, so the catalog entry should carry that caution.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog 5.1 'Central Malay' mala1479 [zlm] is the Greater Riau-Johoric colloquial-Malay node (dialects: Johor, Kuala Lumpur, Melaka, Selangor, Sarawak, Riau, Siak, Riau Sea Tribe, Deli, Sambas, Sedentary Belitung, Melayu Ulu Kapuas, Jambi Pesisir). It is NOT Besemah/'Central Malay' [pse] (= cent2053 South Barisan Malay, already in the catalog via McDonnell 2016); an earlier compilation note naming McDonnell 2016 confused the two. The quoted source, van Wijk 1890, states (Inleiding p.III) that it treats only 'Djohorsch of Riouwsch' (Johor-Riau) Malay, i.e. exactly this node, and is Glottolog's Glottolog's most extensive description long grammar for mala1479. Note overlap risk with the catalog's existing stan1306 'Malay' entry (Winstedt 1913 Malay Grammar, same schwa-conditioned penult rule) and with Zuraidah et al. 2008 / Clynes & Deterding 2011 (no-word-stress analyses of Standard/Malaysian Malay) held under stan1306.

new_statements.quote: In the great bulk of radical words, the accent is on the penultimate. Even adopted foreign words have the accent thrown back to it from the last syllable. The following are examples of the few words which have the accent, not on the penultimate, but the last syllable:—basar, great; basa, because; batul, straight, just; adu, sleep; daram, to sound like thunder; darn [scanned; daru], to roar like the sea; sarang, to assault; sarah, to deliver up; pater, a thunderclap; kara, an ape. Compound words preserve the accents of their radicals. [...] Compound terms and epithets have two accents, as in the words of which they are composed, as mata-ari, the sun; tuwanku, my lord; saarusnalah, justly; mata-ayar, a fountain. (Grammar p.8) — Dissertation p.cix: Accent, in the Malay, the Javanese, and other languages of the west is a very simple and easy matter. In bisyllabic and trisyllabic words, it is, with very few exceptions, on the penultimate, and in polysyllabic words, without exception, there are two accents, one on the first and one on the penultimate syllable.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for mala1479 has an empty rule; the one existing statement (van Wijk 1890 sec.95, read as weight-sensitive) says stress is weak and falls on the penultimate or the last syllable. Crawfurd gives the same two positions with the default made explicit: penultimate in the great bulk of roots, final in a short list of roots that are (in his orthography) schwa-penult words — which is the weight condition behind the weight-sensitive reading, so the two sources are compatible. Crawfurd adds detail the catalog lacks: accent is root-anchored under affixation (antepenult in pandapatan), two accents in polysyllables/compounds (first + penult), and vowel length is a correlate of accent…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Accent falls on the penultimate syllable of the root in the great bulk of words, including loanwords, whose accent is pulled back from the final; a short list of roots take final accent instead. Affixed and compound words keep the accent of their root (adu 'sleep' final-accented -> baradu final, but adukan penult; dapat penult -> pandapatan antepenult), so the accent is fixed to the root rather than counted from the word edge. With a prefixed particle, monosyllabic roots take final accent, with a suffix penultimate (tartra vs trakan). Vowel length is not contrastive: 'an accented vowel is a long, and an unaccented a short one' (p.7).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Polysyllabic words 'without exception' have two accents, one on the first and one on the penultimate syllable (Dissertation p.cix); compound terms and epithets carry the accents of both members (Grammar p.8). Verse lines always have four accented syllables (Prosody p.62).
new_statements.exceptions: Ten listed roots with final accent: basar 'great', basa 'because', batul 'straight, just', adu 'sleep', daram 'to sound like thunder', daru 'to roar like the sea', sarang 'to assault', sarah 'to deliver up', pater 'a thunderclap', kara 'an ape' — in Crawfurd's orthography these mostly have his short a (schwa, printed with a breve the scanned drops) in the penult (bĕsar, bĕtul, dĕram, dĕru, sĕrang, sĕrah, pĕtir, kĕra), though Crawfurd does not state the schwa condition himself. Words like manan 'frankincense' and naning keep first-syllable accent under suffixation (manani).
new_statements.identity_note: Crawfurd 1852 describes 'the Malay language' generally (Grammar based on the written/literary language and speech of the Straits), not the 'Djohorsch of Riouwsch' variety van Wijk names; he remarks that some Malay 'tribes' elide final -k and medial -k, so he was aware of dialect variation but does not localise the accent rule. Glottolog files the work under mala1479. Only vol. 1 (Dissertation and Grammar) was held by the project and read; vol. 2 is the dictionary and was not needed.

readall_conflicts: No real disagreement. Crawfurd 1852 states a penultimate default with a closed list of final-accented roots; van Wijk 1890 (existing statement) says stress is weak and falls on the penultimate or the final syllable. Crawfurd's exceptions are, in his own orthography, mostly schwa-penult roots (bĕsar, bĕtul, dĕram, sĕrang, pĕtir, kĕra), which is exactly the condition the weight-sensitive reading of van Wijk assumes, so the sources agree on placement; they differ only in emphasis (Crawfurd calls accent 'a very simple and easy matter', van Wijk calls it 'zeer zwak'). Crawfurd's root-anchored accent under affixation (adukan penult vs baradu final; pandapatan antepenult) is a detail not in the catalog and not contradicted by anything opened.

sources.citation: Favre, P. 1876. Grammaire de la langue malaise. Vienne: Imprimerie imperiale et royale. Accent rules printed pp.34-35 (archive.org grammairedelalan00favr scanned text).
sources.note: Accent weak, realised as slower/longer syllable; general tendency penultimate: Rule 1 penult open-long or closed -> penult (padang, kilat, bumi, pintu); Rule 2 penult open and short [schwa] -> final (beri, seru, belum, benar); Rule 3 before ng either (dengar, tengah), he prefers penult; suffixed words: either new penult or original root syllable (mendapatkan ~ mendapatkan).

sources.citation: StressTyp2 (2015 SQL dump) entry 'Malay': penult, final if penult schwa; sources Winstedt 1927 Malay Grammar and Lewis 1947 Teach Yourself Malay (already used by our catalog for stan1306).
sources.note: Second-hand: 'Main stress falls on the penult unless this is a schwa, in which case stress falls on the ultima. In Malay only open syllables with schwa are light (Hayes 1995:263)'; remark that Lewis 1947's variety has antepenult stress in heavy-light-heavy words.

sources.citation: Wan Aslynn Salwani Wan Ahmad. 2012. Instrumental phonetic study of the rhythm of Malay. PhD thesis, Newcastle University. Literature review pp.64, 68 (held from the stan1306 check).
sources.note: Reports second-hand that Farid (1980) [Johor Malay], Baskaran (1982), Suhaila (1994) and Teoh (1994) 'claim that, based on auditory observation, there is no systematic variation of syllable prominence in Malay connected speech'; her own experiments: durational penult/final effects in isolated words vanish in connected speech.

sources.citation: Zuraidah Mohd Don, Gerry Knowles & Janet Yong. 2008. How words can be misleading: a study of syllable timing and 'stress' in Malay. The Linguistics Journal 3(2). (Two native speakers of Malaysian Malay, Univ. Malaya; held from the stan1306 check.)
sources.note: Citation forms show an F0 peak on the penult and final lengthening, which looks like penult stress, but in connected speech this is an onset rise + final cadence of the phrase; they conclude Malay 'does not have word stress at all' and disagree with earlier penult-stress claims; schwa penult (betul) delays the peak to the final syllable.

sources.note: 'There is no strong accent on any syllable in a Malay word. Ordinarily the stress, such as it is, falls on the penultimate.. the only important exception being that when the penultimate is e-breve [schwa] in an open syllable and rarely in a closed, then the stress falls on the last syllable, e.g. seri, enam, entah, empat.' Suffixed words: root keeps its stress and the new penult is prolonged (except -kan after consonant-final stem).
